title: Chapter 1: RELATIONS AND FUNCTIONS
subject: Maths
summary: This chapter explores the fundamental concepts of relations and functions, which form the backbone of mathematical modeling and problem-solving. Students will delve into how relations connect elements between sets and classify them based on properties like reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity. The study of functions will cover their classifications—injective, surjective, and bijective—as well as operations like composition and invertibility. By understanding these ideas, learners will develop critical skills in analyzing mappings and transformations, essential for advanced topics in mathematics and real-world applications.

topics.title: Introduction
topics.content:
1. Prerequisites

  • Sets: Understand basic set theory including elements, subsets, and Cartesian products.
  • Relations in Context: Recall how relationships between objects are described in everyday language (e.g., family ties, comparisons).

2. Introduction

Have you ever wondered how mathematicians describe connections between objects? This chapter explores relations and functions, starting with foundational ideas from Class XI. By the end of this section, you’ll understand how to define relations formally, recognize their role in mathematics, and appreciate why functions are a special type of relation.

3. Explanation

3.1 Definition of Relations

A relation from set $ A $ to set $ B $ is defined as a subset of the Cartesian product $ A \times B $. Mathematically, if $ R \subseteq A \times B $, then $ R $ represents a relation.

Example: Let $ A = \{\text{students in Class XII}\} $ and $ B = \{\text{students in Class XI}\} $. A relation $ R $ could be $ \{(a, b) \in A \times B : a \text{ is brother of } b\} $.

3.2 Notation and Membership

  • If $ (a, b) \in R $, we say $ a $ is related to $ b $ under $ R $, written as $ a R b $.
  • Relations abstract away from intuitive connections; they are purely arbitrary subsets of $ A \times B $.

3.3 Functions as Special Relations

Functions are special cases of relations where each element in the domain maps to exactly one element in the codomain. This idea builds on the foundation established in Class XI.

4. Solved Examples

Example 1: Identifying a Relation

Let $ A = \{1, 2, 3\} $ and $ B = \{4, 5\} $. Define $ R = \{(1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 4)\} $.

Solution:

  • Verify $ R \subseteq A \times B $: All elements in $ R $ are pairs from $ A \times B $.
  • Conclusion: $ R $ is a valid relation.

Example 2: Constructing a Relation

Let $ C = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : 1 \leq x \leq 5\} $ and $ D = \{y \in \mathbb{Z} : y > 0\} $. Define $ S = \{(c, d) \in C \times D : c < d\} $.

Solution:

  • Compute $ C = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\} $, $ D = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\} $.
  • Elements of $ S $:

$$ (1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4), ..., (5, 6), (5, 7), ... $$

  • Thus, $ S $ is a valid relation.

5. Practice Problems

🟢 Easy:

  1. Let $ P = \{a, b, c\} $ and $ Q = \{d, e\} $. Is $ T = \{(a, d), (b, e), (c, d)\} $ a relation? Justify.

🟡 Medium:

  1. Define $ U = \{1, 2, 3\} $ and $ V = \{4, 5, 6\} $. Construct a relation $ W \subseteq U \times V $ such that $ (u, v) \in W $ if $ u + v $ is even.

🔴 Hard:

  1. Given $ X = \{1, 2, 3, 4\} $ and $ Y = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\} $, determine the number of possible relations from $ X $ to $ Y $.

Answers:

  1. Yes. $ T \subseteq X \times Y $ because all elements are pairs from $ X \times Y $.
  2. $ W = \{(1, 1), (1, 3), (1, 5), (2, 2), (2, 4), (3, 1), (3, 3), (3, 5), (4, 2), (4, 4)\} $.
  3. The number of relations is $ 2^{n(X \times Y)} = 2^{16} = 65536 $.

6. Summary

  • A relation is a subset of the Cartesian product $ A \times B $.
  • Notation $ a R b $ means $ (a, b) \in R $.
  • Functions are special relations where each input maps to exactly one output.
  • Relations can be constructed based on arbitrary criteria (e.g., age, location, familial ties).

7. Key Formulas

FormulaDescription
$ R \subseteq A \times B $Definition of a relation from $ A $ to $ B $
$ a R b \iff (a, b) \in R $Notation for relation membership
$ n(R) \leq n(A \times B) $Maximum size of a relation

8. Related Topics

  • 1.2 Types of Relations — Explore classifications like reflexive, symmetric, and transitive relations.
  • 1.3 Types of Functions — Study injective, surjective, and bijective functions.
  • 1.4 Composition of Functions and Invertible Function — Learn how to combine functions and identify inverses.

topics.title: Types of Relations
topics.content:
1. Prerequisites

Before diving into this topic, students should already understand:

  • Set notation: Representing sets and their elements using symbols like $A $, $ B $, and $ a \in A $.
  • Cartesian product: Understanding $ A \times A $ as the set of all ordered pairs $ (a, b) $ where $ a, b \in A $.
  • Element membership: Recognizing whether an element belongs to a set (e.g., $ a \in A $ vs. $ a \notin A $).

These foundational concepts are critical for analyzing relations as subsets of $ A \times A $.

2. Introduction

Have you ever wondered how mathematicians describe relationships between objects? In this topic, we explore types of relations—special subsets of $ A \times A $ that exhibit unique properties. By studying these classifications, you’ll gain tools to analyze connections in mathematics, from geometry to computer science.

This section focuses on two extreme relations (empty and universal) and three fundamental types (reflexive, symmetric, and transitive). These ideas form the basis for more advanced topics like equivalence relations and functions.

3. Explanation

3.1 Empty Relation and Universal Relation

Definition 1: A relation $ R $ in a set $ A $ is called an empty relation if no element of $ A $ is related to any element of $ A $, i.e., $ R = \emptyset \subset A \times A $.

Definition 2: A relation $ R $ in a set $ A $ is called a universal relation if every element of $ A $ is related to every element of $ A $, i.e., $ R = A \times A $.

Examples:

  • Consider $ A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\} $ and $ R = \{(a, b) : a - b = 10\} $. Since no pair $ (a, b) $ satisfies $ a - b = 10 $, $ R = \emptyset $ (an empty relation).
  • For $ R' = \{(a, b) : |a - b| \geq 0\} $, all pairs $ (a, b) $ in $ A \times A $ satisfy $|a - b| \geq 0 $, so $ R' = A \times A $ (a universal relation).

These extremes help frame the broader classification of relations.

3.2 Reflexive, Symmetric, and Transitive Relations

Definition 3: A relation $ R $ in a set $ A $ is:

(i) Reflexive if $ (a, a) \in R $ for all $ a \in A $.

(ii) Symmetric if $ (a_1, a_2) \in R $ implies $ (a_2, a_1) \in R $ for all $ a_1, a_2 \in A $.

(iii) Transitive if $ (a_1, a_2) \in R $ and $ (a_2, a_3) \in R $ imply $ (a_1, a_3) \in R $ for all $ a_1, a_2, a_3 \in A $.

Proof of Reflexivity:

To prove a relation $ R $ is reflexive, verify that for every $ a \in A $, the pair $ (a, a) $ exists in $ R $. For example, if $ R = \{(a, b) : a = b\} $, then $ (a, a) \in R $ for all $ a $, satisfying reflexivity.

Proof of Symmetry:

For symmetry, assume $ (a_1, a_2) \in R $. To confirm symmetry, explicitly show that $ (a_2, a_1) \in R $. For instance, if $ R = \{(a, b) : a + b = 5\} $, then $ (a, b) \in R $ implies $ a + b = 5 $, and thus $ b + a = 5 $, meaning $ (b, a) \in R $.

Proof of Transitivity:

Assume $ (a_1, a_2) \in R $ and $ (a_2, a_3) \in R $. To prove transitivity, derive $ (a_1, a_3) \in R $ using the relation’s rule. For example, if $ R = \{(a, b) : a < b\} $, then $ a_1 < a_2 $ and $ a_2 < a_3 $ imply $ a_1 < a_3 $, hence $ (a_1, a_3) \in R $.

3.3 Equivalence Relations

While not explicitly defined in the source, the text hints at equivalence relations as those that are simultaneously reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. This trio of properties ensures that relations partition sets into distinct equivalence classes—a cornerstone of abstract algebra.

4. Solved Examples

Example 1:

Problem: Let $ A $ be the set of all students in a boys’ school. Prove that the relation $ R = \{(a, b) : a \text{ is sister of } b\} $ is empty, and $ R' = \{(a, b) : | \text{height}(a) - \text{height}(b)| < 3 \text{ meters}\} $ is universal.

Solution:

  1. Empty Relation:
  • Since the school is for boys, no student can be a sister of another student.
  • Therefore, $ R = \emptyset $, confirming it is an empty relation.
  1. Universal Relation:
  • Heights of students differ by less than 3 meters due to biological constraints.
  • Thus, $ R' = A \times A $, making it a universal relation.

Example 2:

Problem: Determine if the relation $ R = \{(1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 1)\} $ on $ A = \{1, 2\} $ is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

Solution:

  1. Reflexive:
  • Check if $ (1, 1) \in R $ and $ (2, 2) \in R $.
  • $ (1, 1) \in R $ holds, but $ (2, 2) \notin R $.
  • Conclusion: Not reflexive.
  1. Symmetric:
  • Verify $ (a, b) \in R $ implies $ (b, a) \in R $.
  • $ (1, 2) \in R $ and $ (2, 1) \in R $; $ (1, 1) \in R $ and $ (1, 1) \in R $.
  • Conclusion: Symmetric.
  1. Transitive:
  • Check if $ (1, 2) \in R $ and $ (2, 1) \in R $ imply $ (1, 1) \in R $.
  • Yes, $ (1, 1) \in R $.
  • Conclusion: Transitive.

Example 3:

Problem: Is the relation $ R = \{(1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 3)\} $ on $ A = \{1, 2, 3\} $ transitive?

Solution:

  • Check if $ (1, 2) \in R $ and $ (2, 3) \in R $ imply $ (1, 3) \in R $.
  • Yes, $ (1, 3) \in R $.
  • Conclusion: Transitive.

Example 4:

Problem: Let $ R = \{(a, b) : a \text{ divides } b\} $ on $ A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\} $. Is $ R $ reflexive?

Solution:

  • For all $ a \in A $, check if $ (a, a) \in R $.
  • $ a $ divides $ a $ (since $ a/a = 1 $), so $ (a, a) \in R $.
  • Conclusion: Reflexive.

Example 5:

Problem: Let $ R = \{(a, b) : a > b\} $ on $ A = \{1, 2, 3\} $. Is $ R $ symmetric?

Solution:

  • Suppose $ (a, b) \in R $ implies $ a > b $.
  • For symmetry, $ (b, a) $ must also belong to $ R $, requiring $ b > a $.
  • Contradiction: $ a > b $ and $ b > a $ cannot both hold.
  • Conclusion: Not symmetric.

5. Practice Problems

🟢 Easy

  1. Let $ A = \{1, 2, 3\} $. Is the relation $ R = \{(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)\} $ reflexive?
  2. Prove that the relation $ R = \{(a, b) : a = b\} $ is symmetric.

🟡 Medium

  1. Let $ R = \{(1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 1)\} $ on $ A = \{1, 2\} $. Is $ R $ transitive?
  2. Is the relation $ R = \{(a, b) : a \leq b\} $ on $ A = \{1, 2, 3\} $ reflexive?

🔴 Hard

  1. Let $ R = \{(a, b) : a^2 + b^2 = 1\} $ on $ A = \mathbb{R} $. Is $ R $ symmetric? Justify.

Answers:

1. Solution:

  • For $ R = \{(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)\} $, every $ (a, a) \in R $.
  • Answer: Yes, $ R $ is reflexive.

2. Solution:

  • Assume $ (a, b) \in R $ implies $ a = b $.
  • Then $ (b, a) \in R $ because $ b = a $.
  • Answer: Symmetric.

3. Solution:

  • $ (1, 2) \in R $ and $ (2, 1) \in R $ imply $ (1, 1) \in R $.
  • Answer: Yes, $ R $ is transitive.

4. Solution:

  • For all $ a \in A $, $ a \leq a $ holds.
  • Answer: Yes, $ R $ is reflexive.

5. Solution:

  • If $ (a, b) \in R $, then $ a^2 + b^2 = 1 $.
  • For symmetry, check if $ b^2 + a^2 = 1 $, which is equivalent to $ a^2 + b^2 = 1 $.
  • Answer: Symmetric.

6. Summary

  • Empty Relation: $ R = \emptyset $; no elements are related.
  • Universal Relation: $ R = A \times A $; all elements are related.
  • Reflexive: $ (a, a) \in R $ for all $ a \in A $.
  • Symmetric: $ (a, b) \in R \Rightarrow (b, a) \in R $.
  • Transitive: $ (a, b) \in R $ and $ (b, c) \in R \Rightarrow (a, c) \in R $.
  • Equivalence Relation: Simultaneously reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

7. Key Formulas

FormulaDescription
$ R = \emptyset $Empty relation
$ R = A \times A $Universal relation
$ (a, a) \in R $Reflexive relation
$ (a, b) \in R \Rightarrow (b, a) \in R $Symmetric relation
$ (a, b) \in R $ and $ (b, c) \in R \Rightarrow (a, c) \in R $Transitive relation

8. Student Corner

Common Mistakes

  1. Confusing Empty and Universal Relations:
  • Error: Assuming $ R = \emptyset $ means no elements exist in $ A $.
  • Correction: $ R = \emptyset $ means no pairs satisfy the relation, not that $ A $ is empty.
  1. Misapplying Symmetry:
  • Error: Thinking symmetry requires $ (a, b) \in R $ and $ (b, a) \in R $ for all $ a, b \in A $.
  • Correction: Symmetry applies only when $ (a, b) \in R $ implies $ (b, a) \in R $.

Exam Tips

  • Practice Identifying Properties: Draw diagrams or tables to visualize relations.
  • Check All Conditions: For equivalence relations, always verify all three properties.

Memory Aid

"R.E.S.T."

  • Reflexive: Every element relates to itself.
  • Equivalent: Symmetry ensures pairs mirror each other.
  • Symmetric: Like a mirror image.
  • Transitive: Chains of relations propagate logically.

9. Related Topics

  • 1.1 Introduction — Understands the foundation of relations as subsets of $ A \times A $.
  • 1.3 Types of Functions — Explores functions as special cases of relations with uniqueness constraints.
  • 1.4 Composition of Functions and Invertible Function — Applies relation properties to function composition and invertibility.

E quivalent: Symmetry ensures pairs mirror each other. S ymmetric: Like a mirror image. T ransitive: Chains of relations propagate logically. 9. topics.title: Types of Functions
topics.content:
1. Prerequisites

Before diving into this topic, ensure you are familiar with:

  • Set theory basics: Understanding of set notation ($A $, $ B $), element membership ($\in $), and subsets ($\subset $).
  • Function fundamentals: Knowledge of how functions map elements from domain to codomain, and basic operations like addition/subtraction of functions.
  • Graph interpretation: Ability to visualize simple functions (e.g., linear, constant) and analyze their behavior.

2. Introduction

Have you ever wondered why roll numbers in a class are unique? Or why some tasks require matching inputs to outputs without overlaps? These questions tie into the core idea of types of functions—how functions behave when mapping elements between sets. In this section, we explore three critical classifications of functions: one-one (injective), onto (surjective), and bijective (both one-one and onto). By understanding these distinctions, you’ll gain tools to analyze functional behavior in algebra, calculus, and beyond. This builds on your prior knowledge of relations and prepares you for advanced topics like invertibility and compositions.

3. Explanation

3.1 Definitions

Definition 5: A function $ f: X \to Y $ is one-one (or injective) if the images of distinct elements of $ X $ under $ f $ are distinct. Mathematically, for all $ x_1, x_2 \in X $, $ f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2 $.

>

Definition 6: A function $ f: X \to Y $ is onto (or surjective) if every element of $ Y $ is the image of some element of $ X $. That is, for every $ y \in Y $, there exists an $ x \in X $ such that $ f(x) = y $.

>

Definition 7: A function $ f: X \to Y $ is bijective if it is both one-one and onto.

3.2 Key Observations

  • A one-one function ensures uniqueness: no two inputs share the same output.
  • An onto function covers the entire codomain: every possible output is achieved.
  • A bijective function is reversible (invertible) because it pairs each input with a unique output and vice versa.

3.3 Formal Proof: One-One Function

Theorem: If $ f: X \to Y $ satisfies $ f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2 $, then $ f $ is one-one.

Proof: Assume $ f(x_1) = f(x_2) $. By the contrapositive of the definition, this implies $ x_1 = x_2 $. Thus, $ f $ preserves distinctness of inputs.

3.4 Formal Proof: Onto Function

Theorem: If $ f: X \to Y $ satisfies that for every $ y \in Y $, there exists an $ x \in X $ with $ f(x) = y $, then $ f $ is onto.

Proof: By construction, the range of $ f $ equals $ Y $, fulfilling the definition of surjectivity.

3.5 Visual Interpretation

From the source text’s diagrams (Fig 1.2):

  • One-one functions (like $ f_1 $, $ f_4 $) never map two distinct inputs to the same output.
  • Onto functions (like $ f_3 $, $ f_4 $) ensure every element in the codomain is "hit" by at least one input.
  • Bijective functions (like $ f_4 $) combine both properties: unique mappings and full coverage.

4. Solved Examples

Example 1:

Problem: Determine whether the function $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ defined by $ f(x) = 2x + 3 $ is one-one, onto, or bijective.

Solution:

  1. One-one check: Suppose $ f(a) = f(b) $. Then $ 2a + 3 = 2b + 3 \Rightarrow 2a = 2b \Rightarrow a = b $. Hence, $ f $ is one-one.
  2. Onto check: For any $ y \in \mathbb{R} $, solve $ y = 2x + 3 \Rightarrow x = \frac{y - 3}{2} $. Since $ x \in \mathbb{R} $, $ f $ is onto.
  3. Conclusion: $ f $ is bijective.

Example 2:

Problem: Consider $ f: \{1, 2, 3\} \to \{a, b, c\} $ defined by $ f(1)=a $, $ f(2)=b $, $ f(3)=c $. Is $ f $ one-one or onto?

Solution:

  • One-one: All inputs map to distinct outputs; yes.
  • Onto: Every element in the codomain is covered; yes.
  • Conclusion: $ f $ is bijective.

Example 3:

Problem: Let $ f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z} $ be defined by $ f(n) = n^2 $. Is $ f $ one-one or onto?

Solution:

  1. One-one: Counterexample: $ f(2) = 4 $, $ f(-2) = 4 $. Since $ 2 \neq -2 $ but $ f(2) = f(-2) $, $ f $ is not one-one.
  2. Onto: Not all integers are perfect squares (e.g., $ y = 2 $ has no preimage). Thus, $ f $ is not onto.

Example 4:

Problem: Prove that the function $ f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} $ defined by $ f(n) = 2n $ is one-one but not onto.

Solution:

  1. One-one: Suppose $ f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow 2a = 2b \Rightarrow a = b $.
  2. Not onto: For $ y = 1 $, there is no $ n \in \mathbb{N} $ such that $ 2n = 1 $.

5. Practice Problems

🟢 Easy

Problem 1: Check if $ f: \{1, 2, 3\} \to \{a, b, c\} $ with $ f(1)=a $, $ f(2)=b $, $ f(3)=c $ is one-one, onto, or bijective.

🟡 Medium

Problem 2: Let $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ be defined by $ f(x) = 3x - 4 $. Prove it is bijective.

🔴 Hard

Problem 3: Consider $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ given by $ f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor $ (floor function). Determine if it is one-one, onto, or neither.

Answers:

Problem 1:

  • Answer:
  • One-one: Yes (distinct inputs map to distinct outputs).
  • Onto: Yes (all codomain elements are covered).
  • Conclusion: Bijective.

Problem 2:

  • Answer:
  1. One-one: Assume $ f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow 3a - 4 = 3b - 4 \Rightarrow a = b $.
  2. Onto: For any $ y \in \mathbb{R} $, solve $ y = 3x - 4 \Rightarrow x = \frac{y + 4}{3} \in \mathbb{R} $.
  3. Conclusion: Bijective.

Problem 3:

  • Answer:
  • Not one-one: $ f(1.2) = 1 $, $ f(1.5) = 1 $, but $ 1.2 \neq 1.5 $.
  • Not onto: $ y = 1.5 $ has no preimage since floor values are integers.
  • Conclusion: Neither one-one nor onto.

6. Summary

  • A function is one-one if distinct inputs yield distinct outputs.
  • A function is onto if every codomain element is mapped to.
  • A function is bijective if it is both one-one and onto.
  • Injective functions preserve uniqueness; surjective functions ensure completeness.
  • Bijective functions are invertible.

7. Key Formulas

FormulaDescription
$ f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2 $Condition for one-one (injective) function
For all $ y \in Y $, $ \exists x \in X $ such that $ f(x) = y $Condition for onto (surjective) function
$ f $ is bijective ⇔ $ f $ is one-one and ontoBijective function condition

8. Student Corner

Common Mistakes

  • ❌ Confusing one-one with onto: Ensure you test both conditions separately.
  • ❌ Assuming all linear functions are bijective: Linear functions like $ f(x) = mx + c $ are bijective over $ \mathbb{R} $ only if $ m \neq 0 $.

Exam Tips

  • ✔️ Draw diagrams to visualize mappings and identify overlaps or gaps.
  • ✔️ Always verify the domain and codomain explicitly.

Memory Aid

Rhyme: "Injective, surjective, bijective—unique, complete, and reverse!"

9. Related Topics

  • 1.1 Introduction — Establishes foundational ideas about functions and relations.
  • 1.2 Types of Relations — Connects to function classification via relation properties.
  • 1.4 Composition of Functions and Invertible Function — Builds on bijective functions for invertibility.

topics.title: Composition of Functions and Invertible Function
topics.content:
1. Prerequisites

Before diving into composition of functions and invertible functions, students should be familiar with:

  • Set notation and element membership: Understanding symbols like $ \in $, $ \subset $, and $ \cup $ to describe relationships between elements and sets.
  • Function definitions: Knowing how to represent functions as mappings $ f: A \to B $, including domain, codomain, and range.
  • Basic operations on functions: Recognizing addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of functions (though not explicitly covered here, foundational knowledge aids comprehension).

2. Introduction

Have you ever wondered how multiple processes can be combined to produce a final result? For instance, consider converting temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit and then to Kelvin—each step relies on a function applied to the output of the previous one. This is the essence of composition of functions, a powerful tool in mathematics.

In this topic, we explore how to combine two functions into a single function and understand the conditions under which a function can be "reversed" (invertible). These ideas are vital for advanced topics like calculus, linear algebra, and computer science algorithms. By mastering this, you’ll gain insights into how functions interact and transform inputs systematically.

3. Explanation

3.1 Composition of Functions

Definition: Let $ f: A \to B $ and $ g: B \to C $ be two functions. The composition of $ f $ and $ g $, written as $ g \circ f $, is a new function $ g \circ f: A \to C $ defined by $ (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) $ for all $ x \in A $.

This operation applies $ f $ first, then uses its output as input for $ g $. The order matters: $ g \circ f \neq f \circ g $ in general.

Key Properties of Composition

  • Associativity: If $ h: C \to D $, then $ h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f $.
  • Non-commutativity: $ g \circ f \neq f \circ g $ unless specific conditions are met (see Example 16 below).

3.2 Invertible Functions

Definition: A function $ f: X \to Y $ is invertible if there exists a function $ g: Y \to X $ such that:

$$ g \circ f = I_X \quad \text{and} \quad f \circ g = I_Y, $$

where $ I_X $ and $ I_Y $ are identity functions on $ X $ and $ Y $, respectively. The function $ g $ is called the inverse of $ f $, denoted $ f^{-1} $.

Conditions for Invertibility

  • Bijectivity: A function is invertible if and only if it is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto).
  • Injective: $ f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b $.
  • Surjective: For every $ y \in Y $, there exists $ x \in X $ such that $ f(x) = y $.

Proof Sketch for Bijectivity

If $ f $ is invertible, then $ g \circ f = I_X $ implies $ f $ is injective (since $ f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow g(f(a)) = g(f(b)) \Rightarrow a = b $). Similarly, $ f \circ g = I_Y $ implies surjectivity (every $ y \in Y $ is mapped to via $ f(g(y)) $). Conversely, if $ f $ is bijective, define $ f^{-1}(y) = x $ where $ f(x) = y $; this satisfies $ f^{-1} \circ f = I_X $ and $ f \circ f^{-1} = I_Y $.

4. Solved Examples

Example 1: Composition of Finite Functions

Let $ f: \{2, 3, 4, 5\} \to \{3, 4, 5, 9\} $ and $ g: \{3, 4, 5, 9\} \to \{7, 11, 15\} $ be defined as:

  • $ f(2) = 3 $, $ f(3) = 4 $, $ f(4) = f(5) = 5 $,
  • $ g(3) = g(4) = 7 $, $ g(5) = g(9) = 11 $.

Solution: Compute $ g \circ f $:

  • $ (g \circ f)(2) = g(f(2)) = g(3) = 7 $,
  • $ (g \circ f)(3) = g(f(3)) = g(4) = 7 $,
  • $ (g \circ f)(4) = g(f(4)) = g(5) = 11 $,
  • $ (g \circ f)(5) = g(f(5)) = g(5) = 11 $.

Thus, $ g \circ f = \{(2,7), (3,7), (4,11), (5,11)\} $.

Example 2: Comparing $ g \circ f $ and $ f \circ g $

Let $ f(x) = \cos x $ and $ g(x) = 3x^2 $. Show $ g \circ f \neq f \circ g $.

Solution:

  • $ (g \circ f)(x) = g(\cos x) = 3(\cos x)^2 = 3\cos^2 x $,
  • $ (f \circ g)(x) = f(3x^2) = \cos(3x^2) $.

At $ x = 0 $:

  • $ 3\cos^2(0) = 3(1)^2 = 3 $,
  • $ \cos(3(0)^2) = \cos(0) = 1 $.

Since $ 3 \neq 1 $, $ g \circ f \neq f \circ g $.

Example 3: Finding an Inverse Function

Let $ f: \mathbb{N} \to Y $, where $ Y = \{y \in \mathbb{N}: y = 4x + 3, x \in \mathbb{N}\} $, be defined by $ f(x) = 4x + 3 $. Show $ f $ is invertible and find $ f^{-1} $.

Solution:

  • Step 1: Prove $ f $ is bijective.
  • Injective: Suppose $ f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow 4a + 3 = 4b + 3 \Rightarrow a = b $.
  • Surjective: For any $ y \in Y $, $ y = 4x + 3 \Rightarrow x = \frac{y - 3}{4} \in \mathbb{N} $.
  • Step 2: Define $ f^{-1}(y) = \frac{y - 3}{4} $.
  • Verification:
  • $ f^{-1} \circ f(x) = \frac{4x + 3 - 3}{4} = x $,
  • $ f \circ f^{-1}(y) = 4\left(\frac{y - 3}{4}\right) + 3 = y $.

Hence, $ f $ is invertible with $ f^{-1}(y) = \frac{y - 3}{4} $.

5. Practice Problems

🟢 Easy: Composition of Linear Functions

Given $ f(x) = 2x + 1 $ and $ g(x) = x - 3 $, compute $ g \circ f $ and $ f \circ g $.

Answer:

  • $ (g \circ f)(x) = g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1) - 3 = 2x - 2 $,
  • $ (f \circ g)(x) = f(x - 3) = 2(x - 3) + 1 = 2x - 5 $.

🟡 Medium: Invertibility of a Quadratic Function

Let $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ be defined by $ f(x) = x^2 $. Is $ f $ invertible? Justify your answer.

Answer:

  • $ f $ is not invertible because it fails the horizontal line test: e.g., $ f(2) = f(-2) = 4 $, violating injectivity.

🔴 Hard: Inverse of a Piecewise Function

Let $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ be defined by:

$$ f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 1 & \text{if } x < 0, \\ x^2 & \text{if } x \geq 0. \end{cases} $$

Find $ f^{-1}(y) $.

Answer:

  • For $ y < 1 $: Solve $ 2x + 1 = y \Rightarrow x = \frac{y - 1}{2} $ (valid for $ x < 0 $).
  • For $ y \geq 1 $: Solve $ x^2 = y \Rightarrow x = \sqrt{y} $ (since $ x \geq 0 $).

Thus,

$$ f^{-1}(y) = \begin{cases} \frac{y - 1}{2} & \text{if } y < 1, \\ \sqrt{y} & \text{if } y \geq 1. \end{cases} $$

6. Summary

  • Composition of functions combines two functions into one: $ (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) $.
  • Invertible functions satisfy $ g \circ f = I_X $ and $ f \circ g = I_Y $; they must be bijective (both injective and surjective).
  • Key properties: Composition is associative but not commutative.
  • Inverse function: Defined only for bijective functions; satisfies $ f^{-1}(f(x)) = x $ and $ f(f^{-1}(y)) = y $.

7. Key Formulas

FormulaDescription
$ (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) $Composition of functions $ f $ and $ g $.
$ f^{-1}(y) $Inverse function of $ f $, satisfying $ f(f^{-1}(y)) = y $.
$ I_X(x) = x $Identity function on set $ X $.
$ f $ is injective ⇔ $ f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b $Injectivity condition.
$ f $ is surjective ⇔ $ \forall y \in Y, \exists x \in X $ such that $ f(x) = y $Surjectivity condition.

8. Student Corner

Common Mistakes

  • Mistake: Confusing $ g \circ f $ and $ f \circ g $.

Correction: Always apply the inner function first, then the outer function.

  • Mistake: Assuming all functions are invertible.

Correction: Only bijective functions are invertible; check injectivity and surjectivity.

Exam Tips

  • Practice computing compositions and inverses for linear, quadratic, and piecewise functions.
  • Verify your inverse function by composing it with the original function to confirm identity.

Memory Aid

"Compose First, Invert Later": Remember to apply the inner function first when composing, and ensure the function is bijective before attempting to find its inverse.

9. Related Topics

  • 1.1 Introduction — Establishes the foundational framework of functions and relations.
  • 1.2 Types of Relations — Explores equivalence relations, which intersect with invertibility.
  • 1.3 Types of Functions — Covers injective, surjective, and bijective functions, essential for understanding invertibility.

Summary Composition of functions combines two functions into one: $ (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) $. Invertible functions satisfy $ g \circ f = I_X $ and $ f \circ g = I_Y $; they must be bijective (both injective and surjective). Key properties : Composition is associative but not commutative. Inverse function : Defined only for bijective functions; satisfies $ f^{-1}(f(x)) = x $ and $ f(f^{-1}(y)) = y $. 7. Key Formulas Formula Description $ (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) $ Composition of functions $ f $ and $ g $. $ f^{-1}(y) $ Inverse function of $ f $, satisfying $ f(f^{-1}(y)) = y $. $ I_X(x) = x $ Identity function on set $ X $. $ f $ is injective ⇔ $ f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b $ Injectivity condition. $ f $ is surjective ⇔ $  orall y \in Y, \exists x \in X $ such that $ f(x) = y $ Surjectivity condition. 8. Student Corner Common Mistakes Mistake : Confusing $ g \circ f $ and $ f \circ g $. Correction : Always apply the inner function first, then the outer function. Mistake : Assuming all functions are invertible. Correction : Only bijective functions are invertible; check injectivity and surjectivity. Exam Tips Practice computing compositions and inverses for linear, quadratic, and piecewise functions. Verify your inverse function by composing it with the original function to confirm identity. Memory Aid "Compose First, Invert Later" : Remember to apply the inner function first when composing, and ensure the function is bijective before attempting to find its inverse. 9.
